abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model’s full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.

sections.body: Streaming recognizers feed partial transcripts to live captions, machine translation and voice agents, so each emitted token triggers work. A later revision wastes that work or causes a wrong action. The section defines a stable-prefix streaming model as one whose released text at each time is a prefix of its released text at every later time. This property constrains only output order, not encoders, attention masks or training recipes, and it is treated as separate from accuracy and latency. The paper introduces the Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) and LSP learning, a two-stage recipe that adapts a full-context model without causalizing its encoder or adding attention masks.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Revisions to emitted tokens waste downstream work, so the paper treats output stability as a hard requirement alongside accuracy and latency.

sections.body: The section groups related work by what it controls. Streaming architectures bound acoustic context but do not by themselves guarantee that emitted text is final. Measurement work estimates how often prefixes are revised. Inference-time repairs such as Local Agreement and hold-$n$ commit a common prefix or withhold tokens, but the recognizer keeps revising and agreement is not learned. Hoang et al. train on targets anchored to the full-source translation. The paper's target differs by crediting a raw output only when the whole output is a prefix of the full-audio output. Speech language models time emission against the acoustics, whereas this paper times it against the full-context output.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work measures revisions, applies commit rules at inference, or trains on stable targets, while inference rules leave agreement unlearned.

sections.body: The section fixes notation. Audio is divided into frames of 80 ms, and the full-context output $\bar{y}$ is what the same model produces from the whole utterance, not a human reference. The goals are stable output, word error rate comparable to full-context models of similar size, latency below 500 ms at the smallest chunk sizes, a configurable chunk length, and one model that runs in both streaming and full-context modes. The main challenge is context bounding. Forced-aligner timestamps are insufficient as emission points because later audio often disambiguates a token, so emitting at the timestamp forces a guess. The authors also report residual interference: when audio is fed progressively to a full-context model, the number of correct tokens does not grow monotonically.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Streaming a full-context model is hard because timestamp targets force guesses and newly added audio can disturb earlier tokens.

sections.body: The encoder is frozen, so no causalization or attention masks are used. The train-test mismatch is handled in the decoder by deciding when to commit. The longest stable prefix at time $t$, written $L_t$, is the longest earlier output that is entirely a prefix of the full-context output $\bar{y}$. It is model-admissible, meaning it equals an output the model produced from audio available at $t$, and it never shrinks. Compared with the all-future criterion of McGraw and Gruenstein (2012) and the final-anchored label of Hoang et al. (2026), it credits only whole outputs. This is more conservative and biases the model toward later emission. The base model is Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, with an AuT encoder of 300M parameters and a hidden size of 1,024.
sections.heading: Approach
sections.headline: Freezing the encoder, the method trains the decoder to emit a Wait token whenever the received audio does not determine the next token.

sections.body: Training uses proprietary Chinese and English audio, augmented with noise at signal-to-noise ratios sampled from 10 to 35 dB, reverberation from real or simulated room impulse responses, and language-tag flips for a subset of samples. Streamability is the area under the curve of normalized LSP length against normalized time, computed from LSP targets at 80 ms intervals. On 1,860 Buckeye utterances, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B reaches the highest normalized streamability, 0.493. WhisperRT scores below its full-context base model because its outputs are unstable. The annotation procedure marks stable intervals where the teacher output equals its LSP and labels cuts in the gaps with Wait. The authors state that whether streamability predicts performance on tasks such as simultaneous translation remains open.
sections.heading: Training Data Construction
sections.headline: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B has the highest normalized streamability, 0.493, among the models evaluated on 1,860 Buckeye utterances.

sections.body: Supervised fine-tuning runs for one epoch with cross-entropy on LSP targets and the Wait action, using AdamW with an initial learning rate of $10^{-5}$, 2% warmup, and an effective global batch size of 64. Each example is the full utterance with probability 10%. Otherwise it is a prefix cut, placed inside a stable interval with probability 50% and in a gap otherwise. The encoder attention window is sampled between 1 and 8 seconds. Reinforcement learning applies group relative policy optimization over rollouts of one, two, or four streaming turns. Character error rate is the primary reward. The reward has eight components in total, including penalties for repetitions, language inconsistency and premature continuation. The authors state that the effect of each component requires controlled ablations.
sections.heading: Training
sections.headline: Two stages, supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement learning, train only the language decoder while the encoder and projector stay frozen.

sections.body: At the 160 ms chunk used in the main results, the model performs 6.25 updates per second for each stream. A real-time factor below one requires each update to finish before the next chunk arrives. Four techniques reduce cost without changing the model or the monotonicity constraint. Cache reuse keeps the encoder outputs of completed 8 s windows and their decoder cache entries. Wait-terminated decoding ends an update after pre-fill when the first prediction is Wait. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B regenerates five tokens at every update, which the text says amounts to 31.25 serial steps per second at 160 ms. Bounded context keeps only the most recent completed window. Pre-fill verification checks the revisable suffix instead of regenerating it. The causal interleaved design in Table 2 is a theoretical reference that was not implemented.
sections.heading: Streaming Inference
sections.headline: Cache reuse, Wait-terminated decoding, bounded context and suffix verification reduce per-update cost without changing the trained model.

sections.body: Recognition is scored as English word error rate and Chinese character error rate after standard text normalization, with macro averages over 13 main test sets. Transfer is tested on 18 test sets in ten additional languages, and those scores do not enter the English or Chinese averages. Emission lag is retrospective. For each matched unit, it is the audio time when the prefix becomes permanently stable minus the Qwen force-aligned reference end time. The lag excludes execution, queueing and transport, and the authors state that runtime behavior was not verified here. Table 3 reports that R2T2 with U=1 has the lowest total average error of the ranked configurations. The authors also state that flicker frequency is not measured.
sections.heading: Evaluations
sections.headline: R2T2 with U=1 has a total macro error of 5.76, below all three proprietary systems evaluated, and about 0.6 percentage points above full-context decoding.

sections.body: The paper concludes that a strong full-context ASR model can be adapted to accurate streaming recognition while keeping its pre-trained encoder and projector frozen. LSP supervision and explicit Wait targets train the model to defer uncertain continuations. On the evaluated English and Chinese benchmarks, the authors report that R2T2 closes most of the gap to full-context inference, keeps retrospective emission lag low, and leads the ranked configurations in combined macro error. Gains are reported beyond the two post-training languages. Chunk duration and the provisional-token budget trade recognition against lag at inference without retraining. The authors list deployment performance and broader generalization as priorities for further evaluation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Adapting a full-context model gives stable streaming recognition with transfer beyond training languages, while deployment performance remains open for further evaluation.

sections.body: The appendix explains why the three stable-prefix formulations are not interchangeable. All three are hindsight quantities, so none is observable online. None tests accuracy, because each is anchored to the model's own full-context output rather than a ground-truth transcript. Definition 3 is the all-future criterion of McGraw and Gruenstein (2012), which requires agreement with every later output of the same run. Definition 4 is the final-anchored longest common prefix of Hoang et al. (2026), a running maximum that can name a prefix no single output realized. Definition 5 is the model-admissible prefix used in the paper. Propositions 1 to 4 show that the paper's prefix lies inside the final-anchored one, that the all-future prefix does too, that the all-future and paper's prefixes are incomparable, and that all three coincide on append-only trajectories.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix defines three hindsight prefix criteria, proves their containment and coincidence relations, and treats the longest stable prefix as a learning target.
